pos: n. (1490–1568; last Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, first Duke of Prussia, who turned a crusading state into the first evangelical principality)
etymology: From Old High German Adalbert, bright through nobility; adal, noble, and beraht, bright.
biblical_def: Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach was elected Grand Master of the Teutonic Order in 1510 and governed a monastic military state whose whole justification was holy war. He went to Wittenberg, heard Luther, and in 1525 did what no prince of the age had done: he laid down the Order, took the land as a hereditary duchy under the Polish crown, married, and established the Reformation in Prussia by law. Lutheran Prussia was the first territory in Europe to be organised from the ground up as an evangelical state. He founded the university at Königsberg in 1544, paid for the first books printed in Lithuanian and Old Prussian, and sheltered scholars the Empire had driven out. The dictionary records him with care, because the same man who dissolved a crusading order for the gospel later leaned hard on the Osiandrist party and let a court faction execute men over it. He is a case of the magistrate's office rightly used and then abused, and Scripture gives the standard for both: “For he is the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4), and “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a duke as a sovereign prince or a nobleman next in rank to a prince; a magistrate as a public civil officer invested with executive authority; and to secularize as to convert from sacred to common use.
webster_full: DUKE, n. [L. dux, a leader.] A sovereign prince, ruler of a state called a duchy; in England, one of the highest order of nobility, next below a prince.
MAGISTRATE, n. [L. magistratus.] A public civil officer, invested with the executive government of a city or state.
SECULARIZE, v.t. To convert from spiritual appropriation to common use; to make worldly.
ORDAIN, v.t. [L. ordino.] To appoint; to decree; to establish; to invest with ministerial or pastoral authority.
POWER, n. [L. posse, to be able.] Command; the right of governing; authority; dominion; a ruler or one invested with authority.
scriptures: Rom 13:4

For he is the minister of God to thee for good. But if thou do that which is evil, be afraid; for he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil.
Psa 2:10
Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth.
Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.

And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me.
corruption_summary: The last Grand Master of the Teutonic Order, who dissolved it in 1525, took Prussia as a duchy, and made it the first evangelical state in Europe.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is nearer home. Albert is remembered as a hero of the Reformation and a founder of universities, and he was both; he is also the duke under whom the Osiander controversy turned into a court purge, and whose officers put Johann Funck to death in 1566 for a theological party he himself had favoured. The dictionary refuses the two easy readings — the prince as pure instrument of providence, and the prince as mere opportunist who liked the gospel because it gave him a crown.

The principle to recover is that the magistrate's authority is real, derived, and answerable. It is real: “the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1). It is derived, and therefore limited to the end for which it is given: “For he is the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4). And it is answerable, which is why the Psalm addresses kings as men under instruction rather than as sources of law: “Be wise now therefore, O ye kings: be instructed, ye judges of the earth” (Psa 2:10). A prince who serves the church is a nursing father and no more than that (Isa 49:23); when he begins to settle doctrine by decree he has left his commission.

“the powers that be are ordained of God” (Rom 13:1) — the Order dissolved and the duchy founded, 1525.
“For he is the minister of God to thee for good” (Rom 13:4) — the standard by which his later court purge is judged.

pos: n. (c. 1478–1550; Bishop of Samland, the first bishop anywhere to preach the Reformation from his own cathedral)
etymology: Georg, from Greek Georgios, a husbandman; ge, earth, and ergon, work.
biblical_def: Georg von Polentz had been a soldier and a papal chamberlain before Albert made him Bishop of Samland in 1519. Luther's writings reached him, and on Christmas Day 1523 he went into the cathedral at Königsberg and preached justification by faith alone from his own throne. In January 1524 he issued a mandate to his whole diocese ordering the gospel to be preached plainly, baptism to be administered in German, and the clergy to read Luther. He is, so far as the records go, the first diocesan bishop in Christendom to carry his see over to the Reformation without losing it. Luther dedicated his commentary on Deuteronomy to him. He gave up his temporal lordship in 1525 to attend to preaching and visitation, and ordained the Lithuanian and Polish preachers Albert was recruiting. The dictionary records him because he answers the charge that the Reformation had to break the office of bishop to get a preaching church: here the office itself did the preaching. “apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a bishop as an overseer, a prelate having the charge of a diocese; a diocese as the circuit of a bishop's jurisdiction; and a mandate as an official command or charge.
webster_full: BISHOP, n. [Gr. episkopos, an overseer.] An overseer; a spiritual superintendent; in the primitive church, the pastor of a single church; afterwards, one having charge of a diocese.
DIOCESE, n. [Gr. dioikesis.] The circuit or extent of a bishop's jurisdiction; an ecclesiastical division of a kingdom.
MANDATE, n. [L. mandatum.] A command; an order; a precept; a charge given by a superior.
VISITATION, n. The act of visiting, especially the official visit of a superior to inspect the state of a church or diocese.
OVERSEER, n. One who overlooks; a superintendent; a person who has the care of a work or of a flock.
scriptures: A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
Tit 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood.
Eze 34:2

Son of man, prophesy against the shepherds of Israel, prophesy, and say unto them, Thus saith the Lord GOD unto the shepherds; Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves! should not the shepherds feed the flocks?
corruption_summary: Bishop of Samland from 1519; preached justification by faith from the Königsberg cathedral throne on Christmas Day 1523, the first bishop to take his see over to the Reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live argument is an old and internal one. Episcopalian writers have used Polentz to prove that the Reformation was properly conservative and kept the bishops; presbyterian and baptist writers have hurried past him. The dictionary does neither. Polentz matters not because he kept a title but because he used an office to feed a flock, which is the only thing the New Testament ever asks of an overseer.

The principle to recover is that titles do not make overseers and do not excuse them. Scripture gives the job before the honour: a bishop must be “apt to teach” (1Ti 3:2), and the thing he is to teach is not his own: “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Tit 1:9). Paul puts the overseer under the flock's weight, not above it — “Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) — and Ezekiel names the alternative in one line: “Woe be to the shepherds of Israel that do feed themselves!” (Eze 34:2).

“Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock” (Act 20:28) — he surrendered his temporal lordship in 1525 to preach and visit.

pos: n. (c. 1490–1529; Bishop of Pomesania, who with Polentz carried the Prussian sees into the Reformation)
etymology: Erhard, from Old High German era, honour, and hart, hard or firm; a name meaning firm in honour.
biblical_def: Erhard von Queiss was a canon lawyer who became Bishop of Pomesania in 1523 and almost at once threw the weight of the see behind the gospel. His Themata episcopi Risenburgensis of 1524 is one of the earliest episcopal reform programmes in print: it abolished compulsory celibacy in his diocese, struck out the mass as a sacrifice, cut the parade of ceremonies, and required preaching in the tongue the people spoke. With Polentz he gave Albert two bishops instead of one, and two sees rather than a single contested cathedral, which is much of the reason the Prussian Reformation held. He resigned his temporal lordship in 1525 on the same terms as Polentz and spent his last years in visitation. He died young, in 1529, before the Osiandrist troubles that soured the duchy. The dictionary records him as the clearest case in Prussia of stewardship rather than ownership: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a steward as one entrusted with the management of another's property; a canon as a law or rule of doctrine and discipline; and to reform as to change from worse to better by removing abuses.
webster_full: STEWARD, n. A man employed to manage the affairs or property of another; one entrusted with what is not his own.
CANON, n. [Gr. kanon, a rule.] A law or rule of doctrine or discipline enacted by a council; a dignitary of a cathedral.
REFORM, v.t. [L. reformo.] To change from worse to better; to amend; to correct; to restore to a former good state.
CELIBACY, n. [L. caelebs, unmarried.] An unmarried state; a single life.
KNOWLEDGE, n. A clear and certain perception of that which exists, or of truth and fact; learning; information.
scriptures: Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
Mal 2:7
For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts.
Jer 3:15
And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding.

Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.
corruption_summary: Bishop of Pomesania from 1523, whose 1524 reform articles abolished clerical celibacy and the sacrifice of the mass in his diocese; died 1529.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Queiss raises instead a question the Reformation debated among its own: whether a bishop may reform a diocese by his own act, ahead of a general council and without waiting for the whole church. Queiss did it. The dictionary notes that he did it by publishing his grounds for every parish to read and judge, not by private decree, which is the difference between reform and mere prelacy.

The principle to recover is the stewardship of the ministry. The office is a trust, and the one requirement laid on a trustee is fidelity to the owner's mind: “Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful” (1Co 4:2). What is entrusted is knowledge, and the minister is a mouth and not a source: “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts” (Mal 2:7). The Lord's own promise of pastors is a promise of teaching men — “which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15) — and the account they give is for souls (Heb 13:17).

pos: n. (the Prussian see and peninsula on the Baltic whose cathedral stood at Königsberg; the first diocese in Europe reformed by its own bishop)
etymology: From the Old Prussian tribal name Sambia, latinised Sambia, with German Land, land; the land of the Sambians.
biblical_def: Samland is the blunt peninsula between the Vistula and the Curonian lagoons, the heartland of the Old Prussian tribes conquered by the Teutonic Order in the thirteenth century. Its cathedral stood across the river from the ducal castle at Königsberg, and from its throne Georg von Polentz preached the Reformation in 1523. The diocese then became the working model for everything that followed in the north-east: a reformed cathedral chapter, visitation of the parishes, preaching in German, and before long in Lithuanian and Old Prussian too, because Samland's own people had never spoken German. The first printed book in Lithuanian was made for parishes partly in this diocese. Samland is therefore the place where the Reformation first had to reckon seriously with men who could not read the language of their own church, and answered it by translating rather than by requiring them to learn. Isaiah had said what that costs and what it is worth: “The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light” (Isa 9:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a see as the seat of episcopal power, the diocese of a bishop; a peninsula as land almost surrounded by water; and heathen as a pagan, one who worships idols.
webster_full: SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; a diocese; the jurisdiction of a bishop.
PENINSULA, n. [L. paene, almost, and insula, an island.] A portion of land connected with a continent by a neck, but nearly surrounded with water.
HEATHEN, n. [Saxon haethen.] A pagan; a gentile; one who worships idols, or is unacquainted with the true God.
LIGHT, n. That which renders objects visible; illumination; figuratively, knowledge, instruction, the truth of the gospel.
TONGUE, n. The instrument of taste and speech; a language, the speech of a nation.
scriptures: Isa 9:2
The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined.
Mat 4:16
The people which sat in darkness saw great light; and to them which sat in the region and shadow of death light is sprung up.
For so hath the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.
Zep 2:11
The LORD will be terrible unto them: for he will famish all the gods of the earth; and men shall worship him, every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen.
corruption_summary: The Prussian diocese whose cathedral stood at Königsberg, reformed by its own bishop in 1523 and the first to preach to its people in Lithuanian and Old Prussian.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a live misuse of the history itself. Samland is sometimes produced as an example of the Reformation simply inheriting the fruits of a crusade: the Order conquered the Prussians, and the Lutherans took over the parishes. The first half is true and ugly. The dictionary notes the second half is not: the Order had held the land for two and a half centuries and had still not given the Sambians the Scriptures in their own tongue, and it was the reformed diocese that set about it.

The principle to recover is that the gospel goes to a people in their own speech or it does not go to them at all. Isaiah's word is about a people sitting in the dark, not about a people who need better Latin: “they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined” (Isa 9:2), which Matthew applies to a despised northern district (Mat 4:16). The commission runs outward by design — “I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth” (Act 13:47) — and the end of it is men worshipping God at home, “every one from his place, even all the isles of the heathen” (Zep 2:11).

pos: n. (the second Prussian see, with its cathedral at Marienwerder; reformed by Erhard von Queiss in 1524)
etymology: From Old Prussian pomedian, by the forest; pa, by, and median, forest, latinised as Pomesania.
biblical_def: Pomesania was the inland Prussian diocese along the lower Vistula, with its cathedral at Marienwerder. Its bishop from 1523 was Erhard von Queiss, who in 1524 published reform articles that abolished compulsory celibacy, denied the mass as a propitiatory sacrifice, and ordered plain preaching in the vernacular. Taken together with Samland, Pomesania meant that the Reformation in Prussia came to the people through both of their own bishops rather than against them, which is why there was no cathedral war there and no long interim. When Queiss and Polentz both surrendered their temporal lordships in 1525, their sees were absorbed into the ducal administration and the bishops became what the New Testament calls overseers and nothing else. Pomesania was later resettled in part by Dutch and Frisian Mennonites, and it is also the diocese where Polish-speaking parishes were first served in Polish. The isles that wait for his law in Isaiah are these northern coasts and their hinterland as much as any: “and the isles shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a cathedral as the principal church in a diocese containing the bishop's see; an isle as an island, a tract of land surrounded by water; and vernacular as native, belonging to the country of one's birth.
webster_full: CATHEDRAL, n. [Gr. kathedra, a seat.] The principal church in a diocese, in which is the see or seat of the bishop.
ISLE, n. [L. insula.] A tract of land surrounded by water; in Scripture, often a maritime country or coast.
VERNACULAR, a. [L. vernaculus.] Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as one's vernacular tongue.
ARTICLE, n. [L. articulus, a joint.] A distinct part or clause; a particular of doctrine or of a stipulation.
WAIT, v.i. To stay or rest in expectation; to look for with trust; to attend upon.
scriptures: Isa 42:4
He shall not fail nor be discouraged, till he have set judgment in the earth: and the isles shall wait for his law.
Isa 60:9

Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring thy sons from far, their silver and their gold with them, unto the name of the LORD thy God, and to the Holy One of Israel, because he hath glorified thee.
The kings of Tarshish and of the isles shall bring presents: the kings of Sheba and Seba shall offer gifts.
For so hath the Lord commanded us, saying, I have set thee to be a light of the Gentiles, that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth.
corruption_summary: The inland Prussian see on the lower Vistula, cathedral at Marienwerder, whose bishop Erhard von Queiss published reform articles in 1524.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The honest difficulty with Pomesania is what happened to the office. By 1525 both Prussian bishops had given up their lands and jurisdiction and the sees themselves lapsed into the duke's administration. That was a gain in one direction and a loss in another: the bishop stopped being a territorial prince, and the prince began settling church affairs. Prussia paid for that in the Osiandrist decade, and the dictionary does not pretend otherwise.

The principle to recover is that distant and unconsidered places are in the promise by name. Isaiah does not say the nations will come to be impressed; he says the coasts are waiting for a law they have not yet heard: “and the isles shall wait for his law” (Isa 42:4), and again, “Surely the isles shall wait for me, and the ships of Tarshish first” (Isa 60:9). Kings of far coasts bring tribute to the greater King (Psa 72:10), and the reach of the commission is fixed at the outer edge of the map and nowhere short of it: “that thou shouldest be for salvation unto the ends of the earth” (Act 13:47).

pos: n. (1488–1549; Franciscan doctor turned Prussian reformer, Luther's man at Königsberg and afterwards at Riga)
etymology: Briesmann, a Low German surname from Bries, a place name, with Mann, man; Johann from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johann Briesmann took the Franciscan habit at Cottbus, studied at Frankfurt and Wittenberg, and took his doctorate in theology in 1522 with Luther in the room. He left the Order and went to Prussia in 1523 at Albert's invitation, where he preached in the Königsberg cathedral alongside Polentz and wrote the first evangelical defence published in the duchy, answering the Franciscan Schatzgeyer. He drafted the Königsberg church order, and in 1527 went to Riga to settle the Livonian churches after the disorders there, returning to Prussia in 1531 to spend his last eighteen years as cathedral preacher and president of the Samland chapter. He is the connecting link between the Prussian and the Livonian Reformations, and almost everything stable in either passed through his hands. He had a doctor's chair in an order with a great name and traded it for a frontier pulpit: “But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ” (Php 3:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a friar as a brother or member of a religious order; gain as profit, advantage, interest; and loss as privation, the failure to keep what one had.
webster_full: FRIAR, n. [L. frater, a brother.] A brother or member of a religious order, particularly of the mendicant orders.
GAIN, n. Profit; advantage; interest; something obtained as an advantage.
LOSS, n. Privation; the failure to keep possession; destruction; waste.
ORDER, n. [L. ordo.] Regular disposition; a rule or regulation; a body of men united by a rule; the mode of ecclesiastical discipline.
ESTEEM, v.t. [L. aestimo.] To set a value on, whether high or low; to prize; to regard with reverence.
scriptures: Php 3:7
But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.
Php 3:8

Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord: for whom I have suffered the loss of all things, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ,
Esteeming the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures in Egypt: for he had respect unto the recompence of the reward.
Gal 1:16
To reveal his Son in me, that I might preach him among the heathen; immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood:
corruption_summary: Franciscan doctor who left the Order for Prussia in 1523, wrote the duchy's first evangelical defence, drafted the Königsberg church order, and settled the Riga churches in 1527.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a sentimental reading of men like Briesmann worth refusing: that the monks who left their orders were escaping an unbearable discipline into freedom. Briesmann left a doctorate and a settled house for a frontier diocese, an unfinished church order, hostile neighbours and a plague-ridden city. He did not exchange rigour for ease; he exchanged a false ground of standing for a true one, and kept the rigour.

The principle to recover is that the accounting Paul makes is an accounting, not a mood. He uses the ledger words on purpose: things that were gain are now entered as loss, and the entry is deliberate — “But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ” (Php 3:7), and then, lest it be read as a single resolution, “Yea doubtless, and I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord” (Php 3:8). Moses did the same sum with Egypt on the other side of it (Heb 11:26). And the decision is not a committee's to ratify: “immediately I conferred not with flesh and blood” (Gal 1:16).

pos: n. (1487–1541; Königsberg pastor and hymnwriter, Eck's amanuensis at Leipzig who left him for the gospel)
etymology: Poliander, a Greek rendering of the German surname Graumann; polios, grey, and aner, man.
biblical_def: Johann Poliander, born Gramann, was Johann Eck's secretary at the Leipzig disputation of 1519 and took down Eck's side of the argument against Luther. Hearing it from that seat persuaded him the other way. He studied at Wittenberg, taught at Leipzig and Würzburg, and in 1525 came to Königsberg as pastor of the Altstadt church, where he spent sixteen years building the town's schools, its poor relief and its church order, and arguing hard against the Anabaptists and against Schwenckfeld. He is remembered chiefly for the hymn Nun lob, mein Seel, den Herren, a versification of Psalm 103 made in 1530, which became one of the great congregational psalms of the Lutheran north and is sung still. The dictionary records him because his whole life turns on one psalm text addressed by a man to his own soul: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to bless as to praise, to glorify for benefits received; a benefit as an act of kindness, a favour conferred; and a hymn as a song of adoration to God.
webster_full: BLESS, v.t. [Saxon bletsian.] To praise; to glorify for benefits received; to pronounce a wish of happiness to; to make happy.
BENEFIT, n. [L. beneficium.] An act of kindness; a favour conferred; advantage; profit.
HYMN, n. [Gr. humnos.] A song or ode in honour of God; among pagans, a song in honour of a deity.
SOUL, n. The spiritual, rational and immortal substance in man; the understanding; the vital principle.
AMANUENSIS, n. [L.] A person who writes what another dictates, or copies what another has written.
scriptures: Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits:
Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies;
While I live will I praise the LORD: I will sing praises unto my God while I have any being.
Eph 5:19
Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
corruption_summary: Eck's secretary at the Leipzig disputation who was converted by what he wrote down; pastor at Königsberg from 1525 and author of the Psalm 103 hymn Nun lob, mein Seel, den Herren.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse touches the hymn rather than the man. A psalm-paraphrase of this kind is now often treated as a period piece, a thing the congregation is given to sing because it is old. Poliander wrote it to put a whole psalm in the mouths of people who could not read one, so that the doctrine would be carried home in the memory. A hymn in that use is a catechism with a tune, and swapping it for a chorus with four lines is not a neutral trade.

The principle to recover is the duty a man owes his own soul. The psalm is not a report on feelings; it is a command issued inward, and it names the reason: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2). Forgetting is the sin it guards against, and remembrance is specific — redemption, crowning, mercy: “Who redeemeth thy life from destruction; who crowneth thee with lovingkindness and tender mercies” (Psa 103:4). The duty runs the whole length of a life (Psa 146:2), and Paul puts it in the assembly's mouth in psalms, hymns and spiritual songs (Eph 5:19).

roots_lines: Hebrew barak (H1288) — to kneel, to bless; “Bless the LORD, O my soul”, Psalm 103:2.
Hebrew gemul (H1576) — a recompence, a benefit; “all his benefits”, Psalm 103:2.
Hebrew shakach (H7911) — to forget; “forget not”, Psalm 103:2.
Hebrew ga'al (H1350) — to redeem, to act as kinsman-redeemer; Psalm 103:4.
Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song struck on strings; Ephesians 5:19.
usage: “Bless the LORD, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psa 103:2) — versified in 1530 as Nun lob, mein Seel, den Herren.
“Who redeemeth thy life from destruction” (Psa 103:4) — pastor of the Königsberg Altstadt from 1525.
“While I live will I praise the LORD” (Psa 146:2) — sixteen years of schools, poor relief and church order.

pos: n. (1508–1560; first rector of the university at Königsberg, Latin poet, and Melanchthon's son-in-law)
etymology: Sabinus, a Latin surname taken by the German Schuler; from the Sabine people of ancient Italy.
biblical_def: Georg Sabinus was a Brandenburger who studied at Wittenberg under Melanchthon, married his daughter Anna, travelled in Italy, and taught rhetoric at Frankfurt an der Oder before Duke Albert called him to be the first rector of the new university at Königsberg in 1544. He organised its faculties, drew its statutes largely from Wittenberg, and gave the Prussian church a seminary it had not had. He was a Latin poet of some reputation and a better administrator than theologian, and when the Osiander quarrel broke over the university he handled it badly and left in 1555 for Frankfurt again. The dictionary records him for the thing he did build: a school that trained the men who preached to Lithuania, Poland and Livonia, founded on the premise that learning begins where the schools of the world cannot reach. “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding” (Pro 9:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a rector as a governor or ruler, the head of a university or college; wisdom as the right use of knowledge; and a university as a seminary of learning with power to confer degrees.
webster_full: RECTOR, n. [L. rector.] A ruler or governor; the chief elective officer of some universities; a clergyman who has the charge of a parish.
WISDOM, n. The right use or exercise of knowledge; in Scripture, the knowledge and fear of God, and sincere obedience to his commands.
UNIVERSITY, n. [L. universitas.] An assemblage of colleges; a seminary of learning empowered to confer the honours of degrees.
UNDERSTANDING, n. The faculty of the human mind by which it apprehends truth; knowledge; intelligence.
TRAIN, v.t. To draw along; to educate; to teach and form by practice; to discipline for a particular purpose.
scriptures: Pro 9:10
The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding.
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
Col 2:3
In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.
Pro 22:6
Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it.
corruption_summary: First rector of the Königsberg university in 1544, Melanchthon's son-in-law, who organised the Prussian church's school and then mishandled the Osiander quarrel and left.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is a temptation the dictionary should name, because Sabinus is an example of it. A university founded to serve the church can come to be run for the sake of its reputation, and its rector can treat a doctrinal crisis as a problem of institutional management. That is roughly what happened at Königsberg in the 1550s: the question whether a man is justified by an imputed or an infused righteousness was handled as a dispute between colleagues to be contained.

The principle to recover is that the fear of God is not a devotional supplement to learning but its starting point and its ordering principle: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom: and the knowledge of the holy is understanding” (Pro 9:10). Paul is contemptuous of the alternative, not because learning is bad but because learning cut loose from God cannot deliver what it promises: “Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world?” (1Co 1:20). The treasures the schools are after are real, and they are kept in a Person: “In whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col 2:3).
roots_summary: Hebrew re'shith (H7225), beginning or chief part; Greek sophia (G4678), wisdom.
roots_lines: Hebrew re'shith (H7225) — the beginning, the first, the chief part; Proverbs 9:10.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom, skill, shrewdness; Proverbs 9:10.
Hebrew binah (H998) — understanding, discernment; Proverbs 9:10.
Greek sophia (G4678) — wisdom; 1 Corinthians 1:20 and Colossians 2:3.
Greek thesauros (G2344) — a treasure, a storehouse; Colossians 2:3.
usage: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Pro 9:10) — first rector of the Königsberg university, 1544.
“Where is the wise? where is the scribe?” (1Co 1:20) — a better administrator than theologian.
“Train up a child in the way he should go” (Pro 22:6) — the school that trained preachers for Lithuania, Poland and Livonia.

pos: n. (1518–1566; Königsberg court preacher and chronicler, Osiander's son-in-law, beheaded in the ducal crisis)
etymology: Funck, a German surname from Funke, a spark; Johann from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious.
biblical_def: Johann Funck studied at Wittenberg, came to Königsberg in 1547, married Andreas Osiander's daughter, and became Duke Albert's court preacher and the chief voice of the Osiandrist party in Prussia. Osiander had taught that a man is justified by the indwelling righteousness of Christ rather than by a righteousness imputed to him, and Funck defended it with the duke's favour behind him for nearly twenty years, while the Samland clergy and the university were driven out or silenced. He also meddled far outside the pulpit, in the duke's finances and in the business of the Polish crown, alongside the adventurer Paul Skalich. In 1566 the Prussian estates, with Polish backing, arrested the court party; Funck was tried at Kneiphof and beheaded. His own chronicle of the world, the Chronologia, outlived him. The dictionary records him as a plain warning: “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a courtier as one who attends the court of a prince, and one who flatters to please; a faction as a party in political society combined for a common interest; and a canker as an eating or corroding sore.
webster_full: COURTIER, n. One who attends or frequents the courts of princes; one who courts or flatters in order to please.
FACTION, n. [L. factio.] A party, in political society, combined or acting in union to oppose the government, or another party; dissension; tumult.
CANKER, n. A corroding or eating sore; a disease that eats away the flesh; anything that corrupts or consumes by degrees.
PRIDE, n. Inordinate self-esteem; an unreasonable conceit of one's own superiority.
JUSTIFY, v.t. [L. justus.] To prove or show to be just; in theology, to pardon and clear from guilt, and to accept as righteous on account of the merits of the Savior.
scriptures: Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus;
Gal 2:16

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified.
corruption_summary: Königsberg court preacher and Osiander's son-in-law, who held the duke's ear for the Osiandrist doctrine of justification until the estates arrested the court party and beheaded him in 1566.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The entry does, however, have to resist two bad verdicts. The one makes Funck a martyr of conscience killed by a mob of politicians; the other makes him a swindler whose theology was a cover. Neither is honest. He appears to have believed Osiander's doctrine; he also used a prince's favour to silence men who answered it, and traded on the pulpit for influence in matters that were none of his business. He was executed without a trial worth the name, and that was a crime against him. The doctrine he defended was still wrong.

The principle to recover is the one the Osiandrists lost, and it is the whole hinge of the gospel: the righteousness by which a sinner is accepted is Christ's own, reckoned to him, and not a quality worked up inside him — “Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal 2:16). A false teaching does not stay in the study; Paul uses a surgeon's word for it, “And their word will eat as doth a canker” (2Ti 2:17). And a favoured man near a throne should read his own position with the proverb open: “Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall” (Pro 16:18).

Greek dikaioo (G1344) — to declare righteous, to justify; Galatians 2:16.

Hebrew ga'on (H1347) — pride, arrogance, swelling; Proverbs 16:18.

usage: “Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12) — court preacher at Königsberg from 1547.
“And their word will eat as doth a canker” (2Ti 2:17) — nearly twenty years of Osiandrist ascendancy in Prussia.
“Pride goeth before destruction” (Pro 16:18) — tried and beheaded at Kneiphof, 1566.

pos: n. (1512–1564; Königsberg professor of theology who returned to Rome and wrote against the Reformation he had taught)
etymology: Staphylus, a Greek rendering of the German surname Stapellage or Staffel; from staphule, a bunch of grapes.
biblical_def: Friedrich Staphylus was born in Osnabrück, studied at Wittenberg where he lodged with Melanchthon, and in 1546 became professor of theology at the new university at Königsberg. He was deep in the Prussian church's business for a decade, drafting and disputing. The Osiander controversy broke him: he sided against Osiander, found the duke against him, and in 1552 left for the Empire, where in 1553 he returned to the Church of Rome. Ferdinand I made him an imperial councillor and he spent his last years as a polemicist against the Reformation, arguing from the Lutherans' own divisions that the appeal to Scripture alone must end in endless schism. His Theologiae Martini Lutheri trimembris epitome was answered up and down Germany. The dictionary records him because an apostasy from within the schools is a real event with real arguments, and because Scripture does not flinch from the category: “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb 10:38).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines apostasy as an abandonment of what one has professed; to recant as to retract a declaration or opinion; and schism as a division in a church or among the members of a religious body.
webster_full: APOSTASY, n. [Gr. apostasia, a standing away.] An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.
RECANT, v.t. [L. recanto.] To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay.
SCHISM, n. [Gr. schisma, a rent.] A division or separation in a church or religious body; a rent, a cleft.
WITHDRAW, v.t. To take back; to retire; to recall; to draw from a place or from a party.
PROFESS, v.t. [L. profiteor.] To make open declaration of; to avow; to acknowledge one's belief in.
scriptures: Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him.
For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them.

They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us.
Luk 9:62
And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God.
corruption_summary: Professor of theology at Königsberg from 1546 who left Prussia in the Osiander crisis, returned to Rome in 1553, and wrote against the Reformation for Ferdinand I.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Staphylus did, however, make an argument still in daily use, and it deserves an answer rather than a sneer. He said: you appealed to Scripture against the church, and within thirty years you were at each other's throats over justification in your own university; therefore the appeal cannot stand, and authority must rest somewhere visible. He had watched the Osiandrist quarrel from the inside and he was not inventing the mess. The answer is not that the divisions were small. It is that a true thing is not disproved by the quarrels of those who hold it, and that Rome's own history of contested councils and rival popes rules out the comparison he wanted.

The principle to recover is that drawing back is a real possibility held out as a warning to professors of religion, not an abstraction: “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb 10:38). Peter puts the aggravation plainly — it is worse to have known the way of righteousness and turn from it (2Pe 2:21) — and John reads the departure backwards, as evidence about what the man was all along: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jn 2:19). The Lord's own word is about the direction a man is facing while his hand is on the work (Luk 9:62).
roots_summary: Greek hupostello (G5288), to draw back or shrink; Greek epistrepho (G1994), to turn back.
roots_lines: Greek hupostello (G5288) — to draw back, to shrink from, to withdraw; Hebrews 10:38.
Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, to turn back; “to turn from the holy commandment”, 2 Peter 2:21.
Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to continue, to remain; “they would no doubt have continued with us”, 1 John 2:19.
Greek euthetos (G2111) — well placed, fit, suitable; “is fit for the kingdom of God”, Luke 9:62.
Greek apostasia (G646) — a defection, a falling away; the root behind the English apostasy.
usage: “Now the just shall live by faith” (Heb 10:38) — professor of theology at Königsberg, 1546.
“but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb 10:38) — returned to the Church of Rome in 1553.
“They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jn 2:19) — imperial councillor and polemicist against the Reformation.
